title: Brown Syndrome: The Trochlear Tether
summary: Brown Syndrome, or Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome, is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by a mechanical failure of the eye to elevate in adduction. This comprehensive guide covers the pathomechanism, differential diagnosis, and surgical management of this complex strabismus entity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder where the eyeball is mechanically prevented from moving upward when it is turned toward the nose (adduction). It is primarily caused by an abnormality of the Superior Oblique (SO) tendon-trochlea complex, preventing the smooth passage of the tendon through the trochlear pulley.

branches: Acquired: Iatrogenic (Following SO tuck or scleral buckling)

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Deficient elevation in adduction (Primary Sign).
Normal or near-normal elevation in abduction.
Down-shoot of the eye in adduction.
V-pattern exotropia (divergence in up-gaze).
Compensatory head posture (Chin-up and contralateral head tilt).
Positive 'click' or 'snap' felt by the patient in intermittent cases.
Widening of the palpebral fissure on adduction.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy
Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical proparacaine or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus (usually 6 o'clock and 12 o'clock).
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe into elevation while in the adducted position.
Step 4: Assess for mechanical resistance. In Brown, there is a hard stop.
Step 5: Compare resistance in abduction (should be free).

sections.title: Wright's Grading System
content: Mild: Restricted elevation in adduction; no hypotropia or downshoot in primary position.
Moderate: Restricted elevation in adduction + downshoot in adduction; no hypotropia in primary.
Severe: Marked restriction in elevation in adduction + marked downshoot + hypotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Hess Chart/Lees Screen: Shows constricted field of elevation in adduction.
High-Resolution MRI (Orbits): To visualize SO tendon thickening or trochlear inflammation.
Blood Work: ESR, CRP, RF, and Anti-CCP if inflammatory etiology is suspected.
Prism Cover Test: In 9 cardinal positions of gaze.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Diagnosis: Confirm mechanical restriction via FDT.
Conservative: Observation if no primary position deviation or abnormal head posture.
Medical: Local corticosteroid injection to the trochlear area (for acquired inflammatory cases).
Medical: Systemic NSAIDs for painful 'clicking' cases.
Surgery: Indicated for significant hypotropia in primary position or severe head tilt.
Post-Op: Immediate aggressive duction exercises to prevent adhesion.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Rapid onset of painful motility restriction (Suspect Orbital Myositis).
New onset head tilt in adults (Rule out underlying systemic disease).
Associated Proptosis or Vision Loss (Suspect Neoplasm/Apex Syndrome).
Failure of FDT to show restriction (Re-evaluate for IO Palsy or CN III palsy).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Brown syndrome is 'elevation deficiency in adduction' - remember the SO tendon is too short to allow the eye to go up and in.
The 'True' Brown syndrome is ALWAYS restrictive on FDT.
Simulated Brown Syndrome: Can occur after a scleral buckle or orbital roof fracture.
Surgical overcorrection is common; patients may end up with a Superior Oblique Palsy.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies using high-resolution dynamic MRI have shown that some cases of 'congenital' Brown are actually associated with SO tendon hypoplasia or abnormal pulleys. Additionally, the use of non-absorbable 'Chicken-beak' silicone expanders (Wright's technique) remains the gold standard for reducing the high rate of iatrogenic SO palsy seen with simple tenotomy.
